newsitem.title: POLAND: Russia accepted NATO growth, Polish President says.
newsitem.headline: Russia accepted NATO growth, Polish President says.

text.p: Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski applauded the result of the Helsinki summit between U.S. leader Bill Clinton and Russia's Boris Yeltsin on Friday, saying that Moscow had de facto agreed to NATO's expansion.

"I think that in this basic question, in fact, I stress in fact, Russia has agreed on the expansion of NATO," Kwasniewski said in a statement issued to Reuters by his spokesman Antoni Styrczula soon after the presidents' meeting ended.

Kwasniewski, whose country sees full, rapid NATO entry as a top policy goal, said Poland had not raised objections to the readiness of the United States and NATO countries to sign a special charter with Russia.

"We think that for a lasting system of security in Europe such a charter between an expanded NATO and Russia and Ukraine can be very useful," Kwasniewski said in the initial comments after learning the outlines of the summit's outcome.
"We also have the impression there was a drawing closer of standpoints and that in fact the expansion of NATO is decided," Kwasniewski said.
Poland expects to be among the first new members, with Hungary and the Czech Republic, to be asked at the pact's July summit in Madrid to start NATO entry talks and to join in 1999.
The country was left by its Western allies to domination by the Soviet Union at the end of World War Two and only threw this off in 1989.
Warsaw has been anxious that NATO should not agree on a watered-down NATO membership for new entrants to meet Russian objections that the pact's enlargement threatens its security.
This fear was expressed, while the summit was under way, by the Polish and Czech foreign ministers Dariusz Rosati and Josef Zieleniec meeting near their countries' border.

"We trust that satisfying the aspirations of countries striving for membership in the alliance will be the result of direct negotiations and will not result from any formal pledges by the alliance towards third countries which could create a second-class membership," they said in a statement.
Kwasniewski said he did not consider that Poland would be a second-class member of NATO because the Western pact did not intend to station nuclear weapons or forces on its territory.

"Denmark has a similar situation and no one regards it as a second-class member in NATO," he said, adding that there was no need for such measures now that the world had left behind the past conflict between great power blocs.

"In my view the presence of new countries in NATO is based on the same Rome treaty in which is included a clear assertion concerning security guarantees, mutual relations between countries of NATO, responsibility for the entirety of security in this region and cooperation in commanding these armies jointly," he said.
"So in my view the enlargement of NATO in peaceful conditions is expansion in which the presence of foreign armies and nuclear weapons is not essential." he said.
The Polish foreign minister Rosati told reporters in the Czech town of Rychnov nad Kneznou that he did not expect the summit to end Russian objections of NATO's growth.
"We should anticipate that Russia will continue its anti-NATO rhetoric right up until decisions are taken concerning the expansion of NATO," PAP quoted him as saying.
